strengths: Identifies and formalizes a genuinely novel and safety-relevant failure mode ('3D Mirage') in monocular depth foundation models, supported by a broad survey of SOTA architectures (transformer, diffusion, generative, metric variants), which is a valuable contribution for the robustness community.

The proposed 3D-Mirage benchmark is the first of its kind focused on real-world optical illusions, with careful planar ROI annotation (including nested masks to exclude real objects) and systematic context-restricted crop augmentation; dataset statistics are reported and human-verified.

The Laplacian-based evaluation framework (DCS/CCS) is well-motivated: it directly targets spurious non-planarity and contextual instability, failure modes invisible to MAE/RMSE, and the dual full/crop view design is a clever probe of context dependence.

The Grounded Self-Distillation approach is parameter-efficient (only ~0.7% trainable params) and the ablation study is thorough and honest — particularly the insightful 'No Knowledge Preservation' analysis showing that lower DCS can be deceptive due to indiscriminate flattening, and the training-duration analysis (Tables A-C) showing the forgetting trade-off.

Extensive appendix analyses (Laplacian response plots across model families, failure mode taxonomy such as 'vertical obstacle bias' and 'structural collapse', failure cases in Fig. O) significantly strengthen the empirical characterization.
The paper discusses limitations (planar-only focus, transformer-only mitigation, missing illusion types) and promises public code and benchmark, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: A critical evaluation-design concern: the mitigation is trained on 3D-Mirage samples and then evaluated with DCS/CCS on 'the 3D-Mirage benchmark' (Sec. 5.2, Table 1), but no train/test split is ever stated. If evaluation is on the training samples, the headline 93% reduction may substantially overstate generalization; a held-out split and results on unseen illusion types are needed.

The DCS/CCS metrics are somewhat ad hoc and of questionable cross-model comparability: DCS values mix very different scales (e.g., 2.083e3 for DepthFM vs CCS in the e-3 range), the top10/mean10 aggregates and percentile normalization choices are not justified, and scores between relative and metric models are not directly commensurable — yet Table 1 ranks all models on the same axes.

The benchmark is modest in scale (468 source images / 1,872 augmented views) and sourced from web imagery of street art, with no discussion of collection protocol, licensing, or attribution of the underlying artworks; also, ROIs cover ~49% of image area on average, which may not well represent the driving scenarios (small distant illusions) that motivate the safety framing.

The method is heavily engineered: seven hand-tuned loss weights (α1–α7), a gating MLP with plane mixture, ring regularizers (rf, re, rg), and an entropy/anchor regularization suite — all with limited justification for the specific values; sensitivity to these hyperparameters is not analyzed, hurting reproducibility.

The proposed losses are ablated only against each other; there is no comparison to simpler or external mitigation baselines (e.g., planarity loss alone, replay-based fine-tuning, or defenses against adversarial MDE attacks like [59, 68]), making it hard to judge the necessity of the full complexity.

The HKR loss description contains a conceptual tension: it is described as self-distillation from the student's 'more accurate' crop prediction, yet the crop view is exactly the condition under which models hallucinate most; the interaction between this and the plane-mixture gating network is under-explained.

Generalization of the mitigation is narrow: demonstrated only on DAv2-L, evaluated mainly via ordinal NYU-v2 accuracy (which still drops slightly, 90.13%→89.73%), and acknowledged failures on unseen illusion types (Fig. O); no evidence the tamed model transfers to other backbone families or diffusion-based models.

Occasional overclaiming in the writing ('first end-to-end framework', 'unequivocally', 'full knowledge preservation' for a measurable accuracy drop) and no statistical significance testing or variance reporting for the benchmark results.

strengths: The paper targets a genuine and underexplored safety-relevant failure mode of monocular depth foundation models (hallucinated 3D structure on planar surfaces with ambiguous 2D texture and restricted FOV), and the motivating examples (Fig. 1-2) are compelling and clearly communicate the problem.

The 3D-Mirage benchmark of real-world illusion images with manually annotated planar ROIs and controlled context-restricted crops is a tangible, reusable resource; the annotation protocol (nested ROIs excluding real objects) is thoughtful, and dataset statistics are reported.

The evaluation framework correctly identifies a real weakness of MAE/RMSE-style metrics: they dilute localized structural failures, and the full/crop dual-view comparison for contextual instability is a sensible probe design.

The ablation study (Table 2, Tables A-C, Figs. 6-7, Fig. N) is unusually thorough: it disentangles the roles of the re-editing and preservation losses, shows the deceptive 'No LNKP' variant, quantifies the fine-tuning-vs-LoRA trade-off, and analyzes extended training, which strengthens the internal validity of the mitigation claims.

The appendix contains substantial additional analysis (indoor/outdoor failure regimes, capacity effects, qualitative failure cases), and the limitations discussion is honest (e.g., failure on protrusion illusions, photorealistic long-distance scenes).
weaknesses: Circular evaluation: the Grounded Self-Distillation method is trained on the 3D-Mirage benchmark data and evaluated on the same benchmark with the same Laplacian-planarity quantity that defines the LHKR loss. The headline 93% DCS reduction therefore largely reflects direct optimization of the test metric on its training distribution. There is no held-out set of unseen illusion types, unseen scenes, or a second benchmark to demonstrate that the mitigation generalizes rather than memorizing 'flatten annotated ROIs'. The admitted failures on protrusion/cube illusions (Fig. O) suggest the model learned ROI-specific flattening behavior, not geometric grounding.

The metrics are not validated. DCS and CCS are heuristic composites of Laplacian energies with many arbitrary design choices (top10 vs. mean10 aggregation, per-view 1-99% normalization, two added terms per score). No correlation with human judgment, with ground-truth depth, or with downstream task utility is provided. The wildly different scales across sub-metrics (dcluster ~ hundreds vs. Dcluster ~ 1e-4) and the composite 'sum of two terms' constructions make the reported magnitudes and relative improvements hard to interpret; small CCS deltas (86% of ~1.5e-3) could be noise-sensitive.

The evaluation rewards flattening by construction: the ground truth for an illusion ROI is 'planar', so a degenerate model that outputs constant depth inside any annotated (or detected-similar) region scores perfectly. The paper does not test whether the tamed model retains correct depth for genuinely non-planar content that resembles illusions, i.e., whether the fix trades hallucination for a new failure mode on the open world.

Narrow empirical scope of the mitigation: only one backbone (DAv2-L) is adapted, and the only mitigation baseline is naive full fine-tuning. Missing comparisons include simple alternatives (e.g., fine-tuning with only the NKP term, prompt/adapter variants, test-time ensembling of full and crop views, or classical smoothing-based defenses), making it hard to judge whether the elaborate gated plane-mixture machinery (K fitted planes, gating MLP, seven loss weights) is necessary.

Benchmark scale and coverage are modest: 468 source images / 1,872 samples of street-art-style illusions, acknowledged by the authors to exclude reflective, texture-less, and weather-related ambiguity. The safety-driving motivation (autonomous vehicles) is somewhat overstated given that the benchmark centers on murals and chalk art rather than driving-native decoys.

Presentation and rigor issues: Sec. 4.3 introduces a dense accumulation of rings, seams, guard bands, plane mixtures, and regularizers whose individual contributions are not ablated; the claim of being 'the first' benchmark/framework is asserted repeatedly against a thin comparison to MonoTrap/TartanAir-Adv; data sourcing and licensing for collected street-art images, and the exact train/test split of the benchmark, are not clearly specified, which affects reproducibility and the interpretability of results on 'the test set' (Fig. R/S).

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed problem: the '3D Mirage' failure mode (hallucinated 3D structure from planar but perceptually ambiguous patterns, and context-dependence under restricted FOV) is novel, safety-relevant, and distinct from prior adversarial-depth work.

The 3D-Mirage benchmark is a genuine contribution: 1,872 human-verified real-world illusion images with precise planar ROI masks and controlled context-restricted crops fills a real gap, since KITTI/NYUv2-style benchmarks contain no 'perceptual traps'.

The dual-axis evaluation (DCS for spurious non-planarity, CCS for contextual instability) is a sensible step beyond pixel-wise MAE/RMSE, which the paper convincingly argues are blind to structural failures; the full-vs-crop Laplacian scatter analysis (supplementary) provides good evidence that hallucinations intensify under reduced context.

The Grounded Self-Distillation approach is sensible and parameter-efficient (4M trainable params, ~0.7%), and the ablation study is unusually informative: the No-LNKP variant shows that raw DCS improvement can be deceptive (indiscriminate flattening), which is a good example of qualitative-plus-quantitative validation.

Very broad baseline coverage (16 model variants across transformer, diffusion, generative, and metric/relative families) with extensive supplementary analysis of failure regimes (over- vs under-capacity, indoor/outdoor differences), plus explicit limitations and failure-case discussion.
Clear writing, good figures, and a commitment to releasing code and benchmark, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Train/test circularity in the mitigation evaluation: the student is trained on the same 3D-Mirage samples (4:1 positive sampler) used to report the headline DCS/CCS improvements. There is no held-out split of illusions, no cross-dataset generalization test (e.g., train on chalk art, test on murals), and no comparison against simple baselines (e.g., directly regressing to a planar target in ROI, or a much simpler planarity-only loss). The 93% reduction therefore likely overstates the generalizable fix; the paper should report results on unseen illusion categories.

Metric design is heuristic and under-validated. DCS mixes quantities at very different scales (d_cluster in the hundreds, CCS components ~1e-3), making absolute values hard to interpret; the choices of 1-99% normalization, top-10 vs mean-10 aggregation, and the sum-of-two-terms composition are not ablated, and no human-perception or downstream-task correlation is provided to justify that DCS/CCS track what actually matters for safety.

The mitigation method is heavily engineered — 7 loss weights (α1–α7), a gated K-plane mixture with gating MLP, three ring masks, CE/entropy/anchor regularizers — with weights justified only as 'numerically comparable'. Sensitivity to these choices and the necessity of the plane-mixture machinery (vs. a single planar target) are not demonstrated.

Knowledge-preservation evaluation is thin: NYU-v2 ordinal pairwise accuracy and background R2 on the benchmark's own background regions are weak proxies; no evaluation on KITTI/DA-2K zero-shot relative depth beyond a single supplementary column, and no metric-depth check.

The benchmark is small at the source level (468 images, heavily crop-augmented to 1,872), so crops from the same scene are highly correlated; no annotation-consistency statistics (inter-annotator agreement) or licensing/provenance discussion for street-art imagery is given.

The taming result is demonstrated on a single architecture (DAv2-L teacher); given that Marigold/DepthFM are diffusion-based, the claimed general mitigation strategy remains unverified outside one family, as the authors concede.

Some overclaiming in 'first' claims (MonoTrap and physical 3D adversarial attacks [68] are adjacent, though the real-world-illusion focus does appear distinct); the writing also contains minor issues (units confusion in Table 1 presentation, Fig. 4 caption 'an Student').
